Significance
 While the import of nuclear-
encoded transfer RNAs (tRNAs) 
into the mitochondrion is a 
widespread mechanism, the 
existence of a similar biological 
process has never been 
demonstrated in the second 
endosymbiotic organelle, the 
chloroplast. In the photosynthetic 
land plant Selaginella, around 
two-thirds of the plastidial tRNA 
genes are missing. To 
compensate for this lack, we 
show here, using a high-
throughput sequencing 
approach, that numerous tRNAs 
of nuclear origin are selectively 
imported into chloroplasts. They 
are essential for complementing 
the reading of all codons of the 
universal genetic code and 
enabling plastidial protein 
synthesis. Our data also provide 
evidence for the importance of 
tRNA gene transfer during 
evolution in maintaining 
organelle function.

PLANT BIOLOGY
Extensive import of nucleus-­encoded tRNAs into chloroplasts 
of the photosynthetic lycophyte, Selaginella kraussiana
Christina Berrissoua, Valérie Cognata
, Sandrine Koechlera, Marc Bergdolla, Anne-­Marie Duchênea,1, and Laurence Drouarda,1
Edited by Maureen Hanson, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY; received June 20, 2024; accepted September 25, 2024
Over the course of evolution, land plant mitochondrial genomes have lost many 
transfer RNA (tRNA) genes and the import of nucleus-­encoded tRNAs is essential 
for mitochondrial protein synthesis. By contrast, plastidial genomes of photosynthetic 
land plants generally possess a complete set of tRNA genes and the existence of plas-
tidial tRNA import remains a long-­standing question. The early vascular plants of 
the Selaginella genus show an extensive loss of plastidial tRNA genes while retaining 
photosynthetic capacity, and represent an ideal model for answering this question. 
Using purification, northern blot hybridization, and high-­throughput tRNA sequenc-
ing, a global analysis of total and plastidial tRNA populations was undertaken in 
Selaginella kraussiana. We confirmed the expression of all plastidial tRNA genes 
and, conversely, observed that nucleus-­encoded tRNAs corresponding to these plas-
tidial tRNAs were generally excluded from the chloroplasts. We then demonstrated 
a selective and differential plastidial import of around forty nucleus-­encoded tRNA 
species, likely compensating for the insufficient coding capacity of plastidial-­encoded 
tRNAs. In-­depth analysis revealed differential import of tRNA isodecoders, leading 
to the identification of specific situations. This includes the expression and import of 
nucleus-­encoded tRNAs expressed from plastidial or bacterial-­like genes inserted into 
the nuclear genome. Overall, our results confirm the existence of molecular processes

that enable tRNAs to be selectively imported not only into mitochondria, as previously 
described, but also into chloroplasts, when necessary.
RNA trafficking | oorganelle | plant | evolution | gene transfer
 Since the endosymbiotic origin of the mitochondrion from an alpha-proteobacterium 
and the plastid from a cyanobacterium, the ancestral bacterial genomes of these organelles 
have undergone extensive gene loss or gene transfer to the nuclear genome ( 1 ,  2 ). 
Nevertheless, the expression of organellar genomes remains crucial. The mitochondrial 
genome still codes for a limited number of necessary subunits of the respiratory chain. In 
photosynthetic land plants, the plastidial genome codes for essential subunits of photo­
systems. Although both organellar genomes have conserved a few genes, the biogenesis 
of the two organelles relies on their capacity to import the majority of their proteins which 
are now nucleus-encoded.
 Similarly, land plant mitochondrial genomes have retained variable and reduced sets 
of transfer RNA (tRNA) genes and the import of nuclear-encoded tRNAs into plant 
mitochondria is essential to compensate for the loss of mitochondrial tRNA genes ( 3 ). 
In contrast, a full set of plastidial tRNA genes is usually found in photosynthetic land 
plants ( 4 ), and, to date, no import of nuclear-encoded tRNAs has been reported in this 
second endosymbiotic organelle. Nevertheless, nonphotosynthetic parasitic plants such 
as Orobanchaceae ( 5 ), Cuscuta ( 6 ), or the orchid Rhizanthella gardneri ( 7 ) possess reduced 
sets of plastid-encoded tRNAs, insufficient for translation. The authors hypothesized that 
the missing tRNAs could be imported into the plastids of these organisms, although this 
has never been demonstrated.
 In the spike moss family of lycophytes, the early vascular plants of the Selaginella genus 
represent an important model for evolutionary studies ( 8 – 10 ). In nonparasitic photosyn­
thetic lycophytes, plastidial genomes are smaller than those of typical land plants. This 
size reduction is associated with the loss of multiple genes, including more than half of 
the essential tRNA genes ( 11 ,  12 ). To compensate for this apparent lack of tRNA genes, 
several hypotheses have been proposed. One hypothesis suggests that C-to-U RNA editing 
can modify tRNAs at their anticodon, allowing them to read different codons ( 13 ). 
However, despite the fact that Selaginella organelles have a large number of C-to-U RNA 
editing sites, none have been reported in the plastidial Selaginella uncinata tRNAs, which 
weakens this hypothesis ( 14 ). It has also been demonstrated that the use of super wobbling 
(thanks to the reading of all four nucleotides in the third codon position by a single tRNA) 
2 of 8   https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2412221121 
pnas.org
can facilitate translation with a reduced tRNA set ( 15 ). Given the 
high number of missing plastidial-encoded tRNAs (e.g., the lack 
of alanine, valine, isoleucine, or proline tRNAs in most Selaginella 
studied so far, ( 12 )), it is difficult to imagine super wobbling being 
sufficient to compensate for this shortfall in Selaginella . Finally, 
based on our knowledge from mitochondria, where tRNA import 
is a widespread process ( 16 ), the most likely hypothesis remains 
the import of nucleus-encoded tRNAs to complement the set of 
missing tRNAs, as already proposed by ( 11 ).
 Here, to test this latter hypothesis, we used Selaginella kraussi-
ana as a model. Its plastidial genome only encodes 11 tRNA genes, 
which correspond to 10 tRNAs, since the tRNAAsn gene is dupli­
cated. Thanks to highly purified chloroplast preparation and a 
high-throughput tRNA sequencing approach, our data support 
the differential and selective import of numerous nucleus-encoded 
tRNAs into the chloroplasts of this photosynthetic plant. This 
population of imported tRNAs likely complements the insuffi­
cient set of expressed plastidial tRNAs. Among the imported 
tRNA species, we also identified tRNAs expressed from plastidial 
or bacterial-like genes that were transferred into the nuclear

genome during evolution. Overall, our data reveal the different 
strategies used by Selaginella to maintain functional plastidial 
translation. 
Results
S. kraussiana Chloroplasts use Plastid-­Encoded and Nucleus-­
Encoded tRNAs. To answer the question of tRNA import into 
chloroplasts, S. kraussiana was chosen as a plant model for three 
reasons. First, the complete sequence of its plastidial genome 
(NC_040926.1) shows the presence of a limited number of 11 
tRNA genes corresponding to 10 amino acids (17). This contrasts 
with the situation observed in land plants such as Arabidopsis 
thaliana or lycophytes of the Lycopodiaceae or Isotaceae genus 
where the number (30 or 29) of plastidial tRNA genes is complete 
or almost complete (Fig. 1A), ensuring an active plastidial protein 
synthesis. Second, the sequence of its nuclear genome has recently 
been obtained (10), allowing tRNA genes to be identified using 
tRNAscan-­SE (18) and through manual curation, as described in 
(4). Briefly, 456 nuclear-­encoded tRNA sequences corresponding to 
46 tRNA isoacceptors (i.e., having the same amino acid specificity 
but distinct anticodons) and 255 tRNA isodecoders (i.e., having 
the same anticodon but distinct sequences) were retrieved. Data 
are freely available in the PlantRNA database (http://plantrna.
ibmp.cnrs.fr/). Finally, among the Selaginellaceae, S. kraussiana is 
relatively easy to grow and can be used to prepare highly purified 
chloroplasts from young leaves (Fig. 1B), which is essential for 
analyzing the S. kraussiana plastidial tRNA population.
 To assess the quality of the chloroplasts’ purification, small 
RNAs extracted from both the total and plastidial fractions 
( Fig. 1B ) were analyzed by northern blots ( Fig. 1C ). Three probes 
directed against plastid-encoded 5S rRNA, tRNAPhe , or tRNATyr 
showed a strong signal in the plastidial RNA fraction, suggesting 
that tRNA genes encoded by the plastidial genome are expressed. 
On the contrary, a strong signal corresponding to the nucleus- 
encoded tRNAPhe is observed in the total sample. However, almost 
no tRNAPhe is detected in the chloroplast fraction, indicating that 
this tRNA remains in the cytosol. This also shows that the plasti­
dial fraction is not significantly contaminated by nonimported 
cytosolic tRNAs and can be considered a pure plastidial fraction. 
It is also worth noting that the mitochondrial genome of S. kraus-
siana no longer contains any 5S rRNA or tRNA genes ( 19 ). 
Therefore, contamination by mitochondrion-encoded tRNA is 
not possible. Finally, two probes directed against nucleus-encoded 
tRNAThr or tRNAAla were used. These tRNAs have no plastidial 
counterpart. Signals were observed in both fractions, indicating 
that these two tRNAs are not only present in the cytosol but also 
imported into chloroplasts.
 The above data suggest that in S. kraussiana , part of the plasti­
dial tRNA population consists of nucleus-encoded tRNA species. 
The Widespread and Selective Import of Nucleus-­Encoded tRNAs 
into Plastids Enables the Reading of All Universal Codons. The 
next step was to further demonstrate tRNA import into plastids 
and better understand to what extent this import process is 
important for the organelle. To do so, a global qualitative and

quantitative analysis of the total and plastidial tRNA populations 
was conducted. Mim-­tRNAseq, a recently developed and optimized 
high-­throughput tRNA sequencing method (20, 21) for analyzing 
tRNA expression and abundance, was applied to three biological 
replicates of total tRNA fractions, as well as three replicates 
of plastidial tRNA fractions (SI  Appendix, Figs.  S1 and S2). 
Differential analysis between plastidial and total RNA extracts 
allowed us to evaluate, for each tRNA, the enrichment in the 
plastidial fraction. This enrichment is expressed as log2FoldChange 
(Plastid/Total ratio), with a positive value suggesting enrichment in 
the plastidial fraction, and conversely, a negative value suggesting 
depletion (Fig. 2A and SI Appendix, Fig. S3). As expected, the 
10 tRNAs encoded by plastidial genes are expressed and strongly 
enriched in the plastidial fraction (green bars, Fig. 2A).
 Among the 131 nucleus-encoded tRNAs (with a base mean 
value >100 and a mean number of reads in total fractions >10; 
﻿Dataset 1 ), 50 isodecoders have a positive log2 FC with an adjusted 
﻿P﻿-value (P﻿-adj) below 0.05. These tRNAs, enriched in the plasti­
dial fractions, were considered to be imported into the organelles. 
On the contrary, 60 nucleus-encoded tRNA isodecoders, with a 
negative log2 FC and a P﻿-adj below 0.05, were considered to be 
cytosol-specific ( Fig. 2A ). Between these two categories, there are 
21 tRNA species with a log2 FC ranging from −0.48 and 0.59 and 
a P﻿-adj above 0.05. They were considered as “ambiguous” and not 
subjected to further analysis. Nevertheless, for the majority of 
tRNAs, the classification into imported and cytosol-specific cat­
egories likely provides a good indication of the tRNA population 
found in the chloroplasts of S. kraussiana .
 To note, in most cases, nucleus-encoded tRNAs corresponding 
to plastid-encoded tRNAs with the same anticodon are excluded 
from the organelle and instead remain in the cytosol. This exclusion 
is logical, as there is no need to import them (black bars in  Fig. 2 
﻿A and B ). The only notable exception concerns the nucleus-encoded 
tRNAAsn and tRNACys species, which account for 40% and 20% 
of the plastidial tRNA population, respectively. This observation 
may indicate an intermediate situation, suggesting that prior the 
loss of a plastid-encoded tRNA gene, there is a period of redun­
dancy where this tRNA coexists with its nucleus-encoded coun­
terpart imported from the cytosol. Nevertheless, as a whole, a 
differential import of nucleus-encoded tRNAs into the chloroplasts 
of S. kraussiana is observed, and the required tRNAs are imported.
 Knowing that the 10 plastid-encoded tRNAs can only read 18 
codons of the universal genetic code (green boxes in  Fig. 2C ), we 
wondered whether the population of nucleus-derived tRNAs pres­
ent in the plastids is sufficient to complement this incomplete set 
of plastid-encoded tRNAs. Assuming conventional coding/decod­
ing rules ( 22 ) apply here, we searched for nucleus-encoded tRNAs 
that enable the reading of the remaining 44 codons (Note that for 
the AUG codon, two tRNAs are necessary: the elongator and the

initiator tRNAsMet ). As shown in  Fig. 2A (hatched bars), 34 tRNA 
isodecoders imported into the plastids are sufficient to read the 44 
codons. Only a tRNASer UGA is not enriched in the plastidial 
fraction, but the presence of a tRNASer AGA, where the A34 is 
modified to inosine (SI Appendix, Fig. S4A﻿ ), should enable the 
reading of the UCA codon ( 23 ). Overall, our data provide evidence 
that S. kraussiana plastids import a large pool of nucleus-encoded 
tRNAs, which should be sufficient to read all sense codons and 
enable organellar protein synthesis.
 As indicated above, 60 nucleus-encoded tRNAs were consid­
ered depleted in the plastidial fraction, and 15 of them correspond 
to tRNAs for which an equivalent encoded by the plastidial 
genome exists. The remaining 45 depleted tRNAs are isodecoders 
of the 34 tRNA species found enriched in the plastid fraction. In 
many cases, when one tRNA isodecoder is efficiently imported

into the plastids, most of the other tRNA isodecoders of the same 
family are not ( Fig. 2D ). This can be observed, for example, with 
the different tRNAGln , tRNAIle , tRNALys , tRNAMet , tRNAPro , or 
tRNAVal isoacceptors. This observation suggests that certain tRNA

isodecoders are more prone to enrichment in the organelle, indi­
cating the existence of a differential import process not only at 
the level of tRNA isoacceptors but also at a finer level.
 To explain such differential tRNA import, several hypotheses 
can be proposed. Non-exhaustively, this includes the expression 
level of each tRNA isodecoder, their extent of posttranscriptional 
modifications, the identity of modified nucleotides, or their 
sequences. The enrichment of tRNAs does not show any bias based 
on expression level, and often, the most highly expressed tRNA is 
not the most enriched in plastids (SI Appendix, Fig. S5 ). Therefore, 
it suggests that the first hypothesis is unlikely to be valid. Eukaryotic 
tRNAs are usually highly modified with, on average, 13 modified 
nucleotides per tRNA ( 24 ). The mim-tRNAseq method allows 
quantitative profiling through modification-induced misincorpo­
ration tRNA sequencing ( 20 ). A dozen of tRNA modifications 
(e.g., methylation such as m1 A, m1 G, m3 C, or m2﻿2 G or modifica­
tions such as inosine or acp3 U) are efficiently identified using this 
approach. No differences in terms of identity or level of modifica­
tion were observed between tRNAs from plastidial and total frac­
tions, as well as between tRNA isodecoders. This suggests that 
these modifications are not involved in the selectivity of the import 
process. However, as many modifications read by the reverse tran­
scriptase used in the mim-tRNAseq method are silent ( 20 ), we 
cannot exclude the possibility that differences in the modification 
status exist between imported and cytosol-specific tRNAs. Finally, 
sequence alignments between tRNA isodecoders analyzed in  Fig. 2 
show significant sequence variations between the most enriched 
and the most depleted tRNA in the plastidial fraction ( Fig. 2E in 
blue, and SI Appendix, Fig. S6A﻿ ). For instance, the tRNAAla AGC 
or tRNALys UUU show differences of 18 and 20 nt, respectively, 
between the most and least enriched forms. In contrast, when 
tRNA isodecoders of the same family show minimal variation in 
terms of plastidial enrichment, only a few sequence variations are 
noticeable ( Fig. 2E in gray, and SI Appendix, Fig. S6B﻿ ). Overall, 
this supports the idea that sequence determinants may be impor­
tant, although the reason why remains to be investigated. 
Furthermore, tRNA sequence analysis revealed three notable cases, 
which are described below. 
The Imported tRNAPro Species Have a Plastidial Origin. Among 
the tRNA species expressed from nuclear tRNA genes, two types 
of tRNAPro sequences were identified (SI Appendix, Fig. S7A), 
(PlantRNA; http://plantrna.ibmp.cnrs.fr/). In both cases, 
tRNAPro isoacceptors with UGG, CGG, and AGG anticodons 
exist. A phylogenetic analysis shows that the first type of tRNAPro 
sequences is phylogenetically related to the classical plant nucleus-­
encoded tRNAs of eukaryotic origin (Fig. 3A and SI Appendix, 
Fig. S8A). In contrast, the three tRNA gene sequences belonging 
to the second type of tRNAPro are closely related to plastidial 
tRNAPro gene sequences of other plants. All known plastidial 
genomes (except Selaginella species) code for a single tRNAPro 
gene with a UGG anticodon (4). Thus, our data provide evidence 
that, over evolution, i) the S. kraussiana plastidial tRNAPro UGG 
gene has been transferred to the nuclear genome before being lost 
from its own genome, and ii) it has been triplicated. Following 
mutations at different positions including position 34, it gave rise 
to tRNAPro genes with AGG and CGG anticodons. Together, these 
three genes were thus named plastid-­like (plike) tRNAPro genes. 
As mentioned above and as inferred by mim-­tRNAseq analysis, 
the two types of tRNAPro genes are expressed (Fig. 3B). To note, 
the A34 of plike tRNAProAGG is posttranscriptionally modified

to inosine (I) (SI Appendix, Fig. S4B), similar to its eukaryotic 
tRNAPro counterpart. However, the tRNAsPro of eukaryotic origin 
remains in the cytosol, while only the three plike tRNAsPro are 
significantly enriched in the plastids (Fig.  3B). Interestingly, 
the histograms also show that, in the total tRNA fraction, plike 
tRNAProUGG and CGG are as abundant as the cognate tRNAs 
of eukaryotic origin, suggesting that these plike tRNAsPro are also 
engaged in cytosolic translation.
 In short, a tRNA gene of plastidial origin transferred to the 
nuclear genome can be expressed, and reimported into the plastid 
as an essential species for organellar protein synthesis. 
A tRNAArg of Bacterial Origin Is Mainly Localized Within Plastids. 
Similar to tRNAPro genes, two types of tRNAArgUCU gene 
sequences were retrieved (PlantRNA; http://plantrna.ibmp.cnrs.
fr/), (SI Appendix, Fig. S6B). The first type comprises 8 tRNA 
genes of eukaryotic origin and is related to the classical sequences 
encoded in plant nuclear genomes (Fig.  3B and SI  Appendix, 
Fig. S8B), while the second type contains a single tRNA gene 
sequence. Phylogenetic analysis shows that this tRNA sequence 
is related neither to eukaryotic nor plastidial sequences. On the 
contrary, this tRNAArgUCU gene sequence seems evolutionarily 
close to certain bacterial tRNAArg sequences (Fig.  3A and 
SI Appendix, Fig. S8B). However, since mitochondrial tRNAArg 
genes have been lost from gymnosperms and angiosperms, there 
are only a limited number of mitochondrial tRNAArg sequences 
from photosynthetic organisms (mostly streptophyte algae, green 
or red algae, and bryophytes) available (Fig. 3A and SI Appendix, 
Fig. S8B). These mitochondrial sequences are closely related to 
bacterial sequences. Therefore, we cannot exclude the possibility 
that this S. kraussiana tRNAArgUCU gene derives from the 
ancestral mitochondrial tRNA gene transferred to the nuclear 
genome before being lost from its genome. Mim-­tRNAseq data 
provide evidence that both, the eukaryotic type of tRNAArgUCU 
and the bacterial-­like tRNA (named blike tRNAArg), are expressed. 
However, eukaryotic-­type tRNAsArgUCU remain in the cytosol, 
and only the blike tRNAArgUCU is present in the organelle and 
likely used by the plastidial translation machinery (Fig. 3B). This 
blike tRNAArgUCU accounts for only about 8.3% of all reads 
representing tRNAsArgUCU in the total fraction. If we consider 
that, in this fraction, around 11.7% of the reads come from 
plastidial-­encoded tRNAs, this suggests that the blike tRNAArg 
is not used or is very poorly used in the cytosol.
 Overall, we provide evidence here that a bacterial or a mito­
chondrial gene transfer event occurred in the nuclear genome of 
﻿S. kraussiana during the course of evolution. This led to the acqui­
sition of a functional bacterial-like tRNA that is now likely essen­
tial for plastid protein synthesis. 
tRNAsIle Encoded by Nuclear Genes of Eukaryotic Origin with 
a CAU Anticodon Are Used in Both the Cytosol and Plastids. 
Finally, another remarkable feature can be observed within tRNAIle 
species. The nuclear genomes of photosynthetic organisms encode 
isoacceptor tRNAIle genes with AAU and UAU anticodons (http://
plantrna.ibmp.cnrs.fr/). The tRNAIle AAU allows for the reading 
of the AUU and AUC codons, while the tRNAIleUAU, allows for 
the reading of the third isoleucine codon AUA. Using tRNAscan-­
SE 2.0 (18), 19 tRNAIleAAU genes were retrieved from the S. 
kraussiana nuclear genome used in this study (https://sk.ccgg.

fun/), but no tRNAIleUAU gene was detected. A second annotation 
based on another independent assembly of the S. kraussiana nuclear 
genome (NCBI GCA_001021135.1) confirmed these results, 
namely, the absence of tRNAIleUAU genes. Finally, to fully exclude 
PNAS  2024  Vol. 121  No. 46 e2412221121 
https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2412221121 5 of 8
the possibility of having missed tRNAIleUAU gene sequences, the 
read sequences from the mim-­tRNAseq analysis of S. kraussiana 
total RNA fractions were tentatively mapped on plant consensus 
tRNAIleUAU gene sequences retrieved from the PlantRNA 
database without any success. Once more, this confirms that no 
tRNAIleUAU is expressed from the S. kraussiana nuclear genome.
 To explain this result, two nonexclusive hypotheses exist. Either 
the nucleus-encoded tRNAIle AAU can read the UAU codon, which 
is highly possible considering that the A34 is posttranscriptionally 
modified into inosine (SI Appendix, Fig. S4C﻿ ), or another tRNAIle 
capable of decoding the AUA codon is present in this organism.
 Considering the second possibility, we searched for such a 
tRNA. Intriguingly, we identified 7 nucleus-encoded tRNA genes 
that are phylogenetically related to tRNAIle AAU genes but have a 
CAU anticodon. These genes were shown to be expressed in the 
mim-tRNAseq analysis (PlantRNA database;  Fig. 3B and SI Appendix, 
Fig. S8C﻿ ). At the gene level, a CAU anticodon corresponds to a 
tRNAMet and allows for the reading of the AUG codon. Since 
nucleus-encoded initiator tRNAMet and elongator tRNAMet genes, 
with different sequences, are present and expressed in S. kraussi-
ana , no additional tRNA with a CAU anticodon is needed to 
ensure cytosolic translation.
 However, this situation is similar to that observed in bacteria 
( 25 ) and plant organelles ( 26 ,  27 ), where tRNAs encoded by genes 
with a CAU methionine anticodon undergo a conversion into 
tRNAIle during tRNA processing. This conversion is achieved 
through the modification of the C34 into Lysidine (L) in eubacteria 
or its derivative (L*) in plant organelles. Importantly, this single

Discussion
 In this paper, we have analyzed the tRNA population from the 
photosynthetic lycophyte, S. kraussiana, and demonstrated the 
efficient import of approximately 50 nucleus-encoded tRNA iso­
decoders into the plastids of this early vascular plant. In Selaginella 
species, the plastidial genome is smaller, with significant gene 
losses, including numerous tRNA genes, compared to the highly 
conserved plastidial genome of typical land plants. While we can­
not rule out the existence of other processes such as super wob­
bling or editing, this import process of tRNAs of different genetic 
origins ( Fig. 4 ) appears essential and sufficient to complement the 
incomplete set of plastidial tRNA genes and enable active orga­
nellar protein synthesis essential for photosynthetic activity. 
 To date, no tRNA import into the chloroplasts of photosyn­
thetic land plants has been observed. Typically, their plastidial 
genomes encode a complete set of tRNAs, so tRNA import is, a 
priori, not necessary. Selaginella species are phylogenetically placed 
at the base of land plant evolution, between mosses and ferns. 
One possibility is that tRNA import into chloroplasts developed 
recently in the Selaginella lineage, with these plants evolving their 
own specific RNA import mechanism. Alternatively, the presence 
of tRNAs of nuclear origin in their chloroplasts could suggest that, 
early in land plant evolution, tRNA import into chloroplasts was 
feasible. This raises the possibility of a cryptic plastidial tRNA 
import process that emerged early in evolution and is active when 
necessary.This cryptic tRNA import process could also be active 
in nonphotosynthetic parasitic angiosperms such as Orobanchaceae 
( 5 ), Cuscuta ( 6 ), or the orchid R. gardneri ( 7 ) that share the com­
mon feature to lack part of their plastidial tRNA genes and where 
tRNA plastidial import was envisaged. Finally, many ferns appear 
to lack various plastidial tRNA genes ( 28 ,  29 ), and we propose

here that the import of nucleus-encoded tRNA species is also 
taking place to compensate for this lack. The import of tRNAs 
into Selaginella chloroplasts, which we describe here, might rep­
resent a process much more widespread than previously thought 
in the plant world.
 This tRNA import appears to be highly selective. With a few 
exceptions, unnecessary tRNAs, such as those whose equivalents 
are expressed in the plastid genome, are not imported into the 
organelle. This situation is reminiscent of that in mitochondria, 
where the import of a specific population of tRNAs is often linked 
to the population of tRNAs not expressed by the mitochondrial 
genome ( 30 ,  31 ), or not required due to biased codon usage ( 32 ). 
Plastid genomes of different Selaginella species do not encode the 
same sets of tRNA genes. Thus, different sets of imported tRNA 
species are expected if the same rules as for mitochondria exist. 
This would be interesting to study in the future. Nevertheless, 
plastidial enrichment of nuclear-encoded tRNAAsn and tRNACys 
are observed while the corresponding plastidial-encoded tRNA 
genes are still present and expressed. Such cases where plastidial- 
encoded and nuclear-encoded tRNAs with the same anticodon 
exist redundantly within the plastids might be explained by the 
necessity of a gradual process during evolution. In this case, a 
nuclear-encoded tRNA is first acquired and checked for its func­
tionality within the organelle before completely losing the corre­
sponding plastidial gene. Such a step-by-step process is likely 
essential and was recently discussed for tRNA mitochondrial 
import in Silene species ( 3 ).
 In addition to the substantial loss of plastidial tRNA genes, the 
mitochondrial genomes of Selaginella no longer contain any 
tRNA-coding genes ( 19 ). These photosynthetic plants thus rep­
resent an extreme case of dependence on the nuclear genome 
expression to complete tRNA sets and ensure active organellar 
translational machinery. In S. stautoniana and S. tamariscina , the 
number of plastidial tRNA genes is only 6 ( 12 ), strongly suggest­
ing the possibility of finding a lycophyte species entirely devoid 
of plastid and mitochondrial tRNA genes, relying solely on the 
import of nuclear-encoded tRNAs. From a selectivity import point 
of view, more tRNA species have to be imported into mitochon­
dria as more tRNA genes have been lost. However, the extent to 
which the mitochondrial and plastidial tRNA populations share 
common nuclear-encoded tRNAs is presently unknown. For 
instance, it would make sense to also find in mitochondria the 
nucleus-encoded tRNAsPro and tRNAArg of prokaryotic origin, 
which are imported into chloroplasts.
 Cytosolic tRNAs are imported into the mitochondria of numer­
ous eukaryotic cells, and we now provide evidence for plastidial 
tRNA import. While protein import mechanisms have been 
described in great detail in both organelles, the mechanistic ques­
tion of tRNA import processes remains largely unknown. In mito­
chondria, three different models have been proposed. In plants, 
based on in vitro experiments, a “direct import model” has been 
proposed, where naked tRNAs would be translocated at the level 
of the outer membrane through the Voltage-dependent anion 
channel (VDAC) without the need for protein factors ( 33 ). No 
information is available on the passage through the inner mem­
brane. In contrast, a “coimport model” has been described for the 
import of a single tRNALys in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae , 
involving the precursor of the mitochondrial lysyl-tRNA synthetase 
Fig. 4.   An evolutionary model describing the different means used by the 
photosynthetic plant S. kraussiana to ensure functional protein synthesis 
in the cytosol and plastids. In the course of evolution, on one hand, new 
functional nuclear genes have been acquired by intracellular transfer (IGT) of 
a plastidial gene (tRNAProUGG) or by horizontal transfer (HGT) of a bacterial 
gene (tRNAArgUCU). In this latter case, acquisition by IGT of a mitochondrial 
gene cannot be ruled out and is also hypothesized. Duplication of nuclear 
tRNA genes, followed by mutations, particularly at the anticodon, has led to

the generation of new tRNAs (e.g., tRNAIleCAU). On the other hand, several 
plastidial tRNA genes have been lost and their lack is now compensated by 
the import of nucleus-­encoded tRNAs of various origins (eukaryotic, plastidial, 
and bacterial or mitochondrial) into chloroplasts. This import is selective and 
not all nucleus-­encoded tRNAs are found in the organelle.

( 34 ,  35 ). This RNA–protein coimport occurs through the protein 
translocase complexes of the outer (TOM) and inner (TIM) mem­
branes. Although it is assumed that the two macromolecules are 
maintained together during the translocation, it remains unclear 
how this can be achieved, considering that precursor proteins need 
to be unfolded as they pass through the TOM and TIM channels. 
Similarly, a precursor protein can be used as a shuttle to efficiently 
introduce various RNAs, including tRNAs, in plants and mam­
malian cells ( 36 ). Although this system appears artificial, it also 
supports the idea that mitochondria can use carrier proteins, at 
least to efficiently address the RNA at the surface of the mitochon­
dria, and some components of the protein import machinery such 
as the TOM translocase at the level of the outer membrane. 
Finally, the most detailed tRNA import process has been described 
in the mitochondria of the protozoan Trypanosoma brucei where 
an “alternate tRNA import model” has been demonstrated ( 37 , 
 38 ). In this model, tRNAs are translocated through the ATOM40 
pore at the outer membrane and through the integral TIM core 
module of the inner membrane. However, neither the protein 
import 
receptors 
ATOM47 
and 
ATOM69, 
nor 
the 
presequence-associated import motor are required for mitochon­
drial tRNA import. As a whole, the data exclude a “coimport” 
model and show that both macromolecules, tRNA and proteins, 
use the same pathways but alternatively. Like mitochondria, over 
95% of plastidial proteins are encoded by nuclear genes and need 
to be transported into the organelle. The mechanistic of protein 
import into chloroplasts is generally very similar to that in mito­
chondria. Briefly, the primary pathway involves the translocation 
complexes TOC and TIC for the outer and inner envelope mem­
branes respectively, although alternative routes also exist ( 39 ,  40 ). 
While the TOC complex is well characterized, the TIC complex 
is not as well understood ( 41 ). Nevertheless, considering our cur­
rent knowledge of mitochondrial tRNA import, it is tempting to 
speculate that there is no specific pathway dedicated to tRNA 
translocation in chloroplasts. Instead, it is possible that at least 
some of the components of the TOC/TIC complexes are involved 
in the import of this second type of macromolecules. This hypoth­
esis will need to be further investigated in the future, as long with 
the intriguing question of tRNA selectivity.
 Among the nucleus-encoded tRNA species imported into chlo­
roplasts are tRNAsPro of plastidial origin. The transfer of genetic 
material between organellar genomes and the nuclear genome has 
been well documented. Specifically, numerous fragments of mito­
chondrial or plastidial DNA have been found, and the process of 
DNA transfer from organelles to the nucleus persists ( 42 – 46 ). 
However, in the majority of cases, the integration of mitochondrial 
or plastidial sequences into the nucleus does not yield a functional 
nuclear gene because the necessary eukaryotic elements for expres­
sion are absent despite the rapid evolution of these sequences ( 47 ). 
So far, to our knowledge, no organellar-like tRNA gene has been 
shown to be expressed from a nuclear genome. As mentioned above, 
it may be due to the absence of essential elements required for their 
expression, but a second reason is the inability to differentiate 
between true organellar tRNAs and organellar-like tRNAs. In 
Selaginella, the classic single tRNAPro UGG gene found in land 
plant plastidial genomes has been lost. This loss allows for visuali­
zation of the expression of the plastid-like nuclear tRNA gene.

Interestingly, this gene has been triplicated, followed by mutations 
that allow for the acquisition of the three proline anticodons typ­
ically found in eukaryotic tRNAsPro . Nuclear tRNA genes are tran­
scribed by RNA polymerase III and typically contain highly 
conserved A and B internal promoter boxes. Transcription effi­
ciency also depends on upstream elements such as the presence of 
TATA-like motifs and CAA triplets in the −1 to −10 region. 
Additionally, short runs of T residues downstream of tRNA genes 
are essential for terminating transcription and the polyU tail sta­
bilizes the primary tRNA transcripts ( 48 – 50 ). As shown in 
﻿SI Appendix, Fig. S10 , the three plastid-like tRNAsPro genes have 
conserved A and B internal boxes, a downstream T-stretch, and for 
two out of three, a CAA upstream motif. This appears sufficient 
for their transcription and processing to mature tRNAs. Interes­
tingly, these plastidial-like tRNAsPro are likely used not only in the 
chloroplasts but also in the cytosol along with their eukaryotic 
counterparts. Are these tRNAs recognized by the same prolyl-tRNA 
synthetase? Are the plastid-like tRNAs specific to a particular set 
of cytosolic mRNAs? These questions need to be addressed in the 
future. Similarly, the prokaryotic-like tRNAArg UCU gene, which 
has been integrated into the nuclear genome has acquired the pos­
sibility to be functional (SI Appendix, Fig. S10 ). This likely occurred 
before the loss of the plastidial tRNAArg UCU. The plastidial 
genome of Selaginella is highly dynamic compared to other plas­
tidial genomes, resulting in instability and a more significant and 
rapid gene loss ( 12 ). The acquisition of functional genes through 
gene transfer appears to counteract this evolutionary process by 
diversifying the mechanisms that enable Selaginella cells to survive. 
Furthermore, the situation observed in tRNAIle supports the same 
conclusion. Our data strongly argue in favor of the replacement of 
nucleus-encoded tRNAIle UAU species by tRNAIle CAU thanks to 
a prokaryotic-like modification of the C at the first position of the 
anticodon into Lysidine. If this modification is indeed Lysidine or 
derivative, the enzyme responsible for this modification is expected 
to still be present in the nuclear genome of this plant, despite the 
loss of the mitochondrial and plastidial tRNAIle CAU genes. The 
bacterial tRNAIle lysidine synthase, named TilS, modifies cytidine 
into lysidine ( 51 ). A Blast search allowed us to identify a gene in 
﻿S. kraussiana that encodes a homologous protein. This protein has 
highly conserved amino acid residues in the catalytic domain found 
in the N-terminal region. (SI Appendix, Fig. S11A﻿ ). By studying 
the crystal structures of Aquifex aeolicus TiLS ( 52 ) and Geobacillus 
kaustophilus TilS complexed with its tRNA ( 53 ), we were able to 
propose a very similar structural model for the S. kraussiana protein 
(SI Appendix, Fig. S11B﻿ ). Transcriptome profiles of S. kraussiana 
(https://sk.ccgg.fun/ ) indicate that this gene is transcribed in var­
ious tissues, suggesting the presence of a functional protein. Finally, 
while predicted organellar TilS from Arabidopsis or rice has an 
N-terminal targeting sequence, the S. kraussiana protein does not. 
Therefore, it is unlikely that the S. kraussiana protein can be tar­
geted to organelles. Altogether, this strongly supports the hijacking 
of a typically prokaryotic enzyme that could modify the nucleus- 
encoded S. kraussiana tRNAIle CAU, which emerged from a eukar­
yotic tRNAIle AAU gene that underwent an anticodon mutation 
during evolution.
 In conclusion, this work demonstrates the import of nucleus- 
encoded tRNAs, from prokaryotic and eukaryotic origins, into 
Selaginella chloroplasts. 
Materials and Methods
Following is a summary of Materials and Methods with details in SI Appendix. 
Purification of chloroplasts from young leaves of S. kraussiana by differential cen-

trifugation and percoll gradient was an adaptation of (54). Total RNA was extracted 
from young leaves by Tri-­reagent, and enriched in RNA of a size smaller than 150 
nt by a LiCl precipitation step as described in (55). Plastidial RNA fractions were 
extracted by Tri-­reagent. Northern blots were performed as described in (56). 
tRNAs were sequenced using an adaptation of the mim-­tRNAseq method and 
data analysis was performed using an adaptation of the dedicated bioinformat-
ics pipeline (19, 20). Nuclear tRNA genes retrieved from the whole genome of 
S. kraussiana by tRNAscan-­SE 2.0 (18), and manually curated as in (4), are accessible
